newsitem.title: USA: Dollar begins firmer in U.S., buoyed by EMU fears.
newsitem.headline: Dollar begins firmer in U.S., buoyed by EMU fears.

text.p: The dollar started the day firmer versus the mark as traders weighed fears about a weak euro against Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer's support for a strong German currrency, dealers and analysts said.
Separately, Bank of England Governor Eddie George's reference to the "exaggerated strength" of sterling pressured the pound, they said.

MCM CurrencyWatch international economist Kevin Harris said there are still worries about what is going to happen with European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) -- whether the euro will be strong enough and EMU will happen on time.

"Even though we had that partial truce between the Bundesbank and the German government, we still worry about holding assets in EMU countries and that's still giving the dollar a bit of a boost," Harris said.

A Bundesbank spokesman said on Wednesday that remarks made by Tietmeyer and Finance Minister Theo Waigel on the outcome of talks about the German government's plans to raise cash by revaluing the central bank's assets correspond with each other.
The dollar opened at 1.7306/09 marks, up from 1.7265/75 marks at Tuesday's close.
Dollar/mark was higher on the "coattails" of dollar/yen and dollar/Swiss, according to Steven Walker, a senior trader at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in New York.
Walker noted that dollar/mark is still in a range and really needs to break above 1.7345/50 to start looking at new highs.
Speaking at a news conference at Interlaken, Switzerland, Tietmeyer had said the Bundesbank is interested in a strong mark in the future.

Harris said the Tietmeyer remark and large offers to sell dollars around 1.7330 marks pulled the dollar back a little bit. He said there was talk of orders from European central banks to sell dollars around 1.7330/50 marks.
Shortly after the opening, the dollar traded below 1.73 marks.
The dollar rose to 116.30/40 yen at the open from 115.98/08 at the previous close.
A trader noted that there were bids to buy dollars below 116 yen from Japanese institutions and day traders.
Still the trader warned the dollar's upside was limited as offers from Japanese exporters and others will likely emerge around 116.70 to 116.90 yen.

Prior to the opening, Bank of England's George told reporters at Interlaken that the immediate problem is to balance the degree of tension between the pressure of domestic demand, which has been running a bit above a sustainable rate, with the exaggerated strength of the exchange rate.
Experts said this comment weighed on sterling.
The British unit opened at $1.6270/80, down from $1.6343/53 at the previous finish.
Elsewhere, the dollar opened at 1.4445/55 Swiss francs, up from 1.4365/75 francs.
But the dollar edged lower to Canadian $1.3752/57 from C$1.3762/67.
The Australian dollar opened at $0.7588/93.
-- Donna Sells 212-859-1668
